claims.text: The untreated starting alloy has a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies.
Internal phase boundaries cause severe dislocation pile-ups that generate local stress concentrations, microcracking, and catastrophic tensile failure.
Adding 2–4 at% Cu will preferentially segregate Cu to the lamellar interfaces.
Cu segregation will form uniform, ultra-thin, ductile interfacial layers between the two lamellar phases.
The segregated ductile element will lower the interfacial energy.
The modified interface will lower the barrier to dislocation transmission across phase boundaries.
Greater dislocation transmission across the interfaces will reduce dislocation pile-up density.
Slip or shearing across coherent lamellar interfaces can alleviate local stress concentration and avoid crack formation.
Reducing pile-ups and local stress concentrations will suppress microcrack nucleation and propagation.
Cu microalloying will significantly increase room-temperature elongation to failure relative to the untreated alloy.
Cu microalloying will maintain or slightly increase yield strength relative to the untreated alloy.
Cu microalloying will maintain or slightly increase ultimate tensile strength relative to the untreated alloy.
A lamellar eutectic high-entropy alloy can combine high room-temperature tensile ductility with high strength.
The proposed effect is applicable under room-temperature tensile loading.
The benefit requires a uniform, ultra-thin interfacial layer and the absence of deleterious phases.
Excess microalloying may form embrittling compounds and prevent the proposed mechanical improvement.
A less than 20% increase in elongation to failure relative to an unmodified control is specified as a falsifying result.
A decrease in strength or persistence of comparable pile-ups and microcracking is specified as a falsifying result.
